q: Which are the four processes of the Finance performance domain?
options: Plan Cost Management, Estimate Costs, Approve Budget, Close Finances
Plan Financial Management, Estimate Costs, Develop Budget, Monitor and Control Finances
Estimate Costs, Develop Schedule, Develop Budget, Validate Costs
Plan Financial Management, Fund Project, Pay Suppliers, Audit Costs
explanation: The Finance domain has three planning processes (Plan Financial Management, Estimate Costs, Develop Budget) and one monitoring and controlling process.

q: Which process produces the cost baseline?
explanation: Develop Budget (older name: Determine Budget) aggregates the estimated costs of activities or work packages to establish an authorized cost baseline.

q: What is the cost baseline?
options: The approved, time-phased project budget, excluding management reserves
The total of all money the organization has available
The first rough estimate in the charter
The actual costs recorded to date
explanation: The cost baseline is the approved version of the time-phased project budget, excluding management reserves. It changes only through formal change control.

q: Work package estimates total $200,000. The contingency reserve is $20,000 and the management reserve is $10,000. What is the cost baseline?
explanation: Cost baseline = cost estimates + contingency reserve = $200,000 + $20,000 = $220,000. Management reserve is not part of the cost baseline.

q: Using the same figures (estimates $200,000, contingency $20,000, management reserve $10,000), what is the total project budget?
explanation: Project budget = cost baseline + management reserve = $220,000 + $10,000 = $230,000.

q: What is a contingency reserve for?
options: Unforeseen work that nobody could identify
Identified risks with planned responses, also called known-unknowns
explanation: Contingency reserve is budget within the cost baseline allocated for identified risks. Management reserve covers unforeseen work (unknown-unknowns).

q: Which statement about management reserve is correct?
options: It is set aside in addition to the cost baseline, for unforeseen work within the project scope
It is part of the cost baseline
It is used for identified risks
It is spent by any team member as needed
explanation: Management reserve is time or money that management sets aside in addition to the baseline and releases for unforeseen work that is within scope.

q: During initiating, with very little information, the project manager gives an estimate of $100,000 with a range of −25% to +75%. What is this type of estimate called?
explanation: A rough order of magnitude (ROM) estimate is made early and has a wide range, typically −25% to +75%. A definitive estimate narrows to about −5% to +10%.
ref: Practice Standard for Project Estimating, 2.4; PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Cost estimates

q: At charter stage a project's cost estimate was a wide range. A year later, with the design finished, the estimates are much tighter. What happens to the accuracy of cost estimates as the project progresses?
explanation: Cost estimates are reviewed and refined as more detail becomes available. The accuracy of an estimate increases as the project progresses through its life cycle.

q: Flooring costs $40 per square meter and 500 square meters are needed. The estimate of $20,000 is an example of:
explanation: Parametric estimating uses a statistical relationship or rate: quantity × cost per unit.

q: Which technique rolls cost estimates up from work packages to control accounts and then to the whole project?
explanation: Cost aggregation sums the estimates by work package in line with the WBS, then for the higher levels such as control accounts, and finally for the entire project.

q: Planned spending for the next quarter is higher than the funds the organization will release in that quarter. Which technique deals with this?
explanation: Funding limit reconciliation compares planned expenditure with funding limits. A variance may require rescheduling work to level out the rate of spending.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Funding limit reconciliation

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Funding limit reconciliation

q: Before work starts, a contractor trains its welders in the correct procedure so that defects do not occur. Training the team in the correct procedure before work starts is which type of quality cost?
explanation: Prevention costs are spent to prevent poor quality: training, documenting processes, proper equipment and time to do it right.

q: A team spends two days testing and inspecting each batch before it is shipped. Testing and inspecting deliverables are examples of which type of quality cost?
explanation: Appraisal costs are spent on evaluating, measuring, auditing and testing. Together with prevention costs they form the cost of conformance.

q: A customer finds a defect after delivery and the company repairs it under warranty. Which type of quality cost is this?
explanation: Failures found by the customer are external failure costs: warranty work, liabilities and lost business. Rework and scrap found by the project are internal failure costs.

q: A batch fails its inspection and the team has to do the work again. Which of the following belongs to the cost of nonconformance?
explanation: The cost of nonconformance is money spent because of failures: rework and scrap (internal), warranty work and lost business (external).
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Cost of quality (CoQ)

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Cost of quality (CoQ)

q: A project has already spent $400,000 and is going badly. When deciding whether to continue, how should the $400,000 be treated?
options: As the main reason to continue
As a sunk cost that should not influence the decision
As part of the management reserve
explanation: Money already spent that cannot be recovered is a sunk cost. Decisions should be based on future costs and benefits only.
ref: The Project Management Answer Book, Chapter 6, Q5

links.label: The Project Management Answer Book, Chapter 6, Q5

q: A company spreads the rent of its head office across all of its projects. Office rent shared by all projects in the company is an example of:
explanation: Indirect costs (overhead) are shared across several projects and cannot be charged to one project alone. Direct costs belong to a single project.
ref: The Project Management Answer Book, Chapter 6, Q8

links.label: The Project Management Answer Book, Chapter 6, Q8

q: Which statement about the financial management plan is correct?
options: It describes how project costs will be estimated, budgeted, managed, monitored and controlled
It contains the approved cost of each work package
It is the same as the cost baseline
It is written at the end of the project
explanation: The financial management plan is the output of Plan Financial Management and gives guidance on how finances will be managed. It contains no cost figures.

q: Project A has a payback period of 2 years. Project B has a payback period of 4 years. Based on payback period alone, which should be chosen?
options: Project B, because longer is better
Either one, because the payback period does not matter here
Neither, because both are too long
Project A, because it recovers the investment sooner
explanation: Payback period is the time needed to earn back the investment, so shorter is better. For ROI, NPV and IRR, higher is better.
ref: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Glossary (Payback Period)

links.label: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Glossary (Payback Period)

q: A project buys a new production building and the machines to go in it. Money invested in buying equipment and buildings is called:
explanation: CapEx is money invested to acquire, upgrade and maintain physical assets. OpEx covers the ongoing costs of running day-to-day operations, such as wages and rent.

q: Which of the following is an output of Monitor and Control Finances?
explanation: Monitor and Control Finances produces work performance information, revenue and cost forecasts and change requests, and may update the cost baseline.
